books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

stimulus.text: Margaret Fuller, a member of Emerson's circle in Concord, published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845. She argued that women, like men, should be free to develop their minds and characters, and she edited the transcendentalist journal The Dial. The photograph shows Fuller in 1846, seated in profile, reading a book on a stand with her hand raised to her forehead.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the lesson script on transcendentalism: Emerson's circle included Margaret Fuller, whose 1845 Woman in the Nineteenth Century fed the Seneca Falls generation. Photograph: daguerreotype of Margaret Fuller by John Plumbe, Jr., 1846 (National Portrait Gallery). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the photograph visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Fuller's argument most directly connects transcendentalism to which later development?

options.text: The building of the transcontinental railroad across the West
options.misconception: Railroads were the era's great project, so it is easy to tie any 1840s idea to them.

options.text: The women's rights movement meeting at Seneca Falls in 1848
The annexation of Texas into the United States
options.misconception: Texas joined the Union in 1845, the year Fuller published, so it is easy to link the two.

options.text: The founding of the Whig Party in the 1830s
options.misconception: The Whigs were the great opposition party, so it is easy to attach any reform idea to them.

rationales.A: Fuller wrote about women's minds and characters, not about rails, engines, or western routes.
rationales.B: Fuller's book fed the Seneca Falls generation, which met three years after it appeared.
rationales.C: Texas annexation was a political and territorial act; Fuller's subject was women's equality.
rationales.D: The Whigs formed in the 1830s around banks and tariffs, not around Fuller's argument about women.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the book forward. Woman in the Nineteenth Century appeared in 1845; ask who read it next.
2. Match the readers to the meeting. The Seneca Falls generation took up Fuller's claim for women in 1848.
Background: Fuller's book is the bridge from transcendentalist self-trust to organized women's rights.
Remember: an idea's children are the movements that quote it a few years later.
